newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine bolsa criticizes YPF share sale abroad.
newsitem.headline: Argentine bolsa criticizes YPF share sale abroad.

text.p: The Buenos Aires Stock Exchange Friday chided the Argentine government and oil company YPF SA for selling only 15 percent of a block of shares this week in the local market.

"The Argentine market could have absorbed much more than the 15 percent of the shares offered, as it has been demonstrated in prior privatizations," the Bolsa told Economy Minister Roque Fernandez in a letter. But the domestic market was offered no chance to present an underwriting plan nor the possibility to participate in a tender to compete with other would-be bidders to place the shares.

Salomon Inc announced Wednesday 96 percent of the 10 percent block was sold for almost $1.0 billion. The 33.8 million shares placed at $29.25 each were owned by YPF employees under a Shared Property Program launched after Argentina's biggest company was privatized in 1993.
Local Banco Comafi and Merchant Bankers Asociados, an Argentine affiliate of Salomon, as well as U.S. Vest Trust Securities LP, also acted as underwriters.
The shares were placed among institutional investors in the United States (70 percent), Europe (15 percent) and Argentina (15 percent), Salomon said.

The sale was hailed as excellent by analysts who said the cut-off price of $29.25 per share was very attractive and that at the same time the deal removed a factor of uncertainty from its stock value.
The bolsa also said selling the shares abroad risked a higher dependency on international capital market movements.
Net proceeds from the sale include $585 million that will be chanelled to cancel the debts of YPF employees with the Argentine state. YPF will get no money from the deal.
The government authorized the sale of the Class C YPF shares in the hands of the company's employees by a decree issued last Friday.
The bolsa urged the government to adopt a privatization policy that offer shares to the domestic market first and then, in case there is surplus supply, offer them abroad.
The state owns another 20 percent of YPF, but the Peronist government of President Carlos Menem says it has no immediate plans to sell.
But some analysts believe that with presidential polls scheduled for 1999, the government may sell all or part of the state's stake to get money to spend on electoral needs.
